title: Matter and Measurement
description: How matter is classified, how its states change, and how to measure and calculate with it.
overview: Chemistry is the study of matter and the changes it undergoes. Before atoms and bonds, we need a shared vocabulary for what matter is, and a shared way of measuring it. Every later chapter relies on both: a quantity without units, or a result with the wrong number of digits, is not a chemical result.

This chapter classifies matter, describes its three common states and the transitions between them, and sets out the measurement skills used throughout the book: SI units, significant figures, dimensional analysis and temperature scales.
objectives: Classify a sample as an element, compound, homogeneous mixture or heterogeneous mixture.
Distinguish physical from chemical properties and changes.
Describe solids, liquids and gases at the particle level, and name each phase change.
Use SI units and prefixes, and calculate density.
Report calculated results with the correct number of significant figures.
Convert between units by dimensional analysis, and between Celsius, Kelvin and Fahrenheit.

sections.title: Classifying matter
body: **Matter** is anything that has mass and occupies space. Matter is classified by whether its composition is fixed and whether it can be separated by physical means.

list: A **pure substance** has a fixed composition and distinct properties. An **element** is a pure substance that cannot be broken into simpler substances by chemical means (iron, oxygen). A **compound** consists of two or more elements combined in a fixed ratio (water, H₂O, is always 11.19% hydrogen by mass).

A **mixture** is a physical combination of substances in variable proportions. A **homogeneous mixture** (a solution) is uniform throughout, like salt water or air. A **heterogeneous mixture** has visibly distinct regions, like granite or oil and water.

body: Mixtures can be separated by physical methods that exploit differences in properties: filtration separates a solid from a liquid, distillation separates liquids by boiling point, and chromatography separates components by how strongly they stick to a surface. Compounds can be broken down only by chemical reactions.

A **physical property** can be measured without changing the identity of the substance: melting point, density, color, conductivity. A **chemical property** describes how a substance changes into another: flammability, or the tendency to rust. In a **physical change**, such as melting ice or dissolving sugar, the substance is the same before and after. In a **chemical change** (a reaction), new substances form. Signs of a chemical change include gas evolution, a precipitate, a color change not caused by dilution, and heat or light given off.

body.warn: Dissolving and melting are physical changes, even though the material seems to vanish or flow. Salt in water is still sodium chloride, and you can recover it by evaporating the water.

sections.title: States of matter and phase changes
body: The three common **states of matter** differ in how freely their particles move, which in turn depends on how strongly the particles attract one another compared with their thermal energy.

head: State
Particles
Shape and volume
Compressibility
rows: Close together, free to slide past one another
Takes the shape of the container, definite volume
Far apart, moving rapidly and randomly
table.caption: The three common states of matter.

body: A fourth state, **plasma**, is a gas in which many atoms are ionized. It makes up stars and lightning, and it is also what glows in a neon sign or a fluorescent lamp.

A **phase change** moves a substance from one state to another with no change in chemical composition. Melting and freezing connect solid and liquid; vaporization and condensation connect liquid and gas; **sublimation** (solid directly to gas) and **deposition** (gas directly to solid) skip the liquid. Dry ice, solid CO₂, sublimes at −78.5 °C and 1 atm, and frost forms by deposition. Evaporation is vaporization from a liquid surface at any temperature; boiling is vaporization throughout the liquid at the temperature where vapor pressure equals the external pressure.

body: Heat absorbed during melting is the enthalpy of fusion, and during vaporization the enthalpy of vaporization. For water, melting 1 mol of ice takes 6.01 kJ, but vaporizing 1 mol takes 40.7 kJ: boiling must separate the molecules completely, while melting only loosens them.

sections.title: Units and measurement
body: A measurement is a number and a unit. Science uses the International System of Units (**SI**), built on seven base units. Four matter most in chemistry.

**Derived units** combine base units: the newton (kg m s⁻²) for force, the pascal (N m⁻², Pa) for pressure and the joule (N m, J) for energy. Chemists also use the liter (1 L = 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³) and milliliter (1 mL = 1 cm³). Prefixes scale a unit by powers of ten:

**Density** is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V. It is an intensive property: it does not depend on how much of the substance there is. Density is used to identify substances and to convert between mass and volume.

example.title: Density from measurements
example.problem: A metal cube measures 2.50 cm on each edge and has a mass of 140.0 g. Find its density.
solution: This matches copper. The result has three significant figures, because the edge length has three.

body.note: Since 2019 the SI defines every unit from fixed physical constants. The mole is defined by fixing Avogadro’s constant, N_{A} = 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹, and the kilogram by fixing Planck’s constant.

sections.title: Uncertainty and significant figures
body: Every measurement has uncertainty. **Accuracy** is how close a result is to the true value. **Precision** is how closely repeated measurements agree with one another. A scale that always reads 0.5 g too high is precise but not accurate.
The **significant figures** of a number are the digits known reliably plus one estimated digit. The rules for counting them:

list: Zeros between nonzero digits are significant (1002 has four).
Leading zeros are not (0.0045 has two).
Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant (2.500 has four).
Trailing zeros in a number with no decimal point are ambiguous; scientific notation removes the ambiguity (1.20 × 10³ has three).
Exact numbers, such as counted items and defined conversions (100 cm = 1 m), have unlimited significant figures.
**Multiplication and division:** the result has as many significant figures as the factor with the fewest.
**Addition and subtraction:** the result has as many decimal places as the term with the fewest decimal places.
Round only at the end. Carry one or two extra digits through intermediate steps.

example.title: Sig figs in practice
solution: (a) The sum is 35.866. The term 0.3 has one decimal place, so the answer is **35.9**.
(b) The product is 6.384. The factor 1.4 has two significant figures, so the answer is **6.4**.
(c) First the subtraction: 6.75 − 6.20 = 0.55, which has two decimal places and two significant figures. Then 0.55 × 3.142 = 1.728, rounded to two significant figures: **1.7**.

body.warn: The count of significant figures is not the same as the number of decimal places. 0.00520 has three significant figures and five decimal places.

check.q: How many significant figures are in 0.004050?
What is 3.46 × 2.1, to the correct number of significant figures?
check.why: The product is 7.266. The factor 2.1 has two significant figures.

sections.title: Dimensional analysis
body: **Dimensional analysis** converts between units by multiplying by conversion factors, each equal to 1. Arrange each factor so that the unit to be removed appears in the opposite position (numerator against denominator), and the units cancel like algebraic symbols. If the units do not work out to the desired unit, the setup is wrong.

example.title: Converting speed
example.problem: Convert 65 mi/h to m/s. (1 mi = 1609.344 m exactly.)
solution: The answer has two significant figures, as 65 does. The defined conversions are exact.

body: When a unit is squared or cubed, so is its conversion factor. To convert 1.00 m³ to liters, use (100 cm / 1 m)³ = 10⁶ cm³ per m³, then 1 L = 1000 cm³, giving 1000 L.

sections.title: Temperature
body: Temperature measures how hot or cold something is. At the particle level, it is proportional to the average kinetic energy of the particles. It is different from **heat**, which is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. A bathtub of warm water holds more thermal energy than a cup of boiling water, though it is at a lower temperature.

Three scales are in common use. The Celsius scale places the freezing and boiling points of water at 0 °C and 100 °C. The Fahrenheit scale places them at 32 °F and 212 °F. The **kelvin** is the SI unit. Its scale starts at **absolute zero**, 0 K, the lowest possible temperature, at which particles have minimum energy. One kelvin is the same size as one degree Celsius.

Kelvin temperatures never take negative values and are written without a degree sign. Chemistry uses kelvins in any equation where temperature is a factor or a divisor, including the gas laws, the Arrhenius equation and ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, because those equations require a scale with a true zero.

quiz.q: A sample of two elements separates only when it is decomposed by electrolysis, and the elements are always found in the same mass ratio. It is a
quiz.why: Fixed composition and separation only by a chemical process define a compound. A mixture has variable proportions and can be separated by physical means.

quiz.q: A student says that sugar dissolving in water is a chemical change because the sugar disappears. What is the best correction?
quiz.a: The sugar is still sugar and can be recovered by evaporating the water, so the change is physical
wrong: It is chemical, because a solid becomes part of a liquid
It is chemical for compounds like sugar but physical for elements
It is physical only if the temperature of the water stays the same
quiz.why: In a physical change the identity of the substance is unchanged. Disappearing from view is not evidence of a new substance.

quiz.q: Which statement describes a chemical property of methane?
quiz.a: It reacts with oxygen and burns
wrong: It is a colorless gas at room temperature
It condenses to a liquid when cooled enough
It is less dense than liquid water
quiz.why: A chemical property describes how a substance changes into other substances. The other options can all be observed without changing methane into anything else.

quiz.q: How do the particles of a liquid compare with those of a solid?
quiz.a: They are about as close together but can slide past one another
wrong: They are much farther apart and move randomly
They are held in fixed positions but vibrate more strongly
They are closer together, which is why a liquid is less compressible
quiz.why: Both condensed phases have particles in contact, so both are nearly incompressible. Only in the liquid are the particles free to move past each other.

quiz.q: Water is heated steadily in an open pot at 1 atm. While it boils, the temperature stays at 100 °C because
quiz.a: the added energy goes into separating molecules, not into raising their average kinetic energy
wrong: boiling is a chemical change that absorbs the heat
the burner heats the water exactly as fast as the pot loses heat
quiz.why: During a phase change the heat overcomes attractions between molecules. Temperature reflects average kinetic energy, which does not change until the phase change is complete.

quiz.q: The enthalpy of vaporization of water is 40.7 kJ/mol. How much heat is needed to vaporize 2.00 mol at its boiling point?
quiz.why: The heat is proportional to the amount: 2.00 mol × 40.7 kJ/mol = 81.4 kJ. The value 12.0 kJ would be the heat to melt 2.00 mol of ice.

quiz.q: Mercury has a density of 13.6 g/mL. What is the mass of 75.0 mL of mercury?
quiz.why: Mass is density times volume: 13.6 g/mL × 75.0 mL = 1020 g. Dividing the volume by the density gives 5.51, which has the wrong units.

quiz.q: A 10 g sample and a 100 g sample of pure copper at the same temperature are compared. Which quantity is the same for both?
wrong: The heat needed to melt the sample
quiz.why: Density is intensive: it does not depend on how much of the substance there is. Volume, atom count and the heat of melting all scale with the amount.

quiz.q: A laser has a wavelength of 650 nm. Expressed in meters this is
quiz.why: Nano means 10⁻⁹, so 650 × 10⁻⁹ m = 6.5 × 10⁻⁷ m. The error 6.5 × 10⁻⁹ comes from dropping the factor 100 in 650.

quiz.q: How many significant figures does 0.0070300 have?
quiz.why: The leading zeros are not significant. The 7, the zero between 7 and 3, the 3 and the two trailing zeros after the decimal point are all significant.

quiz.q: What is 0.0125 g + 2.5 g + 14.07 g, with the correct number of significant figures?
quiz.why: The sum is 16.5825 g. In addition the result keeps the decimal places of the least precise term, 2.5 g, so one decimal place: 16.6 g.

quiz.q: A mass of 12.50 g occupies 4.2 mL. What is the density, with the correct number of significant figures?
quiz.why: In division the result has as many significant figures as the factor with the fewest. The volume has two, so 2.976 rounds to 3.0, and the zero is kept because it is significant.

quiz.q: A student counts 12 beakers, each of mass 3.45 g, and computes the total as 41.4 g. How many significant figures should the total have?
wrong: 1, because the count has no decimal point
4, because the product 41.4 has several digits
quiz.why: Counted numbers are exact and have unlimited significant figures, so only the 3.45 g limits the result.

quiz.q: Four titrations give volumes of 24.51, 24.50, 24.52 and 24.51 mL. The true value is 25.00 mL. The results are
quiz.why: The readings agree closely with one another (precise) but all sit about 0.5 mL from the true value (not accurate), which suggests a systematic error.

quiz.q: A volume of 2.50 L expressed in cubic meters is
quiz.why: One liter is 1 dm³, and 1 dm = 0.1 m, so 1 dm³ = (0.1 m)³ = 10⁻³ m³. Using 0.1 without cubing it gives the error 2.50 × 10⁻¹.

quiz.q: Sulfuric acid has a density of 1.84 g/mL. What is the mass in kilograms of 0.250 L?
quiz.why: 0.250 L × (1000 mL/L) × 1.84 g/mL × (1 kg/1000 g) = 0.460 kg. Dividing by the density instead of multiplying gives the unit-inconsistent 0.136.

quiz.q: A patient's temperature is 98.6 °F. In °C this is
quiz.why: Invert T(°F) = 1.8 T(°C) + 32: subtract 32 first, then divide by 1.8, giving 66.6/1.8 = 37.0 °C. The value 310.2 is the temperature in kelvin.

quiz.q: Which statement about heat and temperature is correct?
quiz.a: A large bath of warm water can hold more thermal energy than a small cup of boiling water
wrong: Temperature measures the total thermal energy in a sample
Heat is the average kinetic energy of the particles
Doubling the Celsius temperature doubles the average kinetic energy
quiz.why: Temperature tracks the average kinetic energy per particle, while total thermal energy also depends on how many particles there are. A doubling statement is valid only for temperature in kelvin.

summary: Matter is a pure substance (element or compound) or a mixture (homogeneous or heterogeneous). Mixtures separate by physical means; compounds only by chemical reactions.
Solids, liquids and gases differ in particle spacing and mobility. A phase change alters the state but not the composition, and the temperature stays constant during it.
SI base units, prefixes and derived units are the common language of measurement. Density is mass divided by volume.
Multiplication and division keep the fewest significant figures. Addition and subtraction keep the fewest decimal places.
Dimensional analysis converts units by multiplying by factors equal to 1.
T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15. Use kelvins in equations that contain temperature.

problems.q: Classify each as element, compound, homogeneous mixture or heterogeneous mixture: (a) stainless steel, (b) sucrose, (c) a salad, (d) neon gas.
problems.solution: Stainless steel is a uniform alloy of iron, chromium and carbon. Sucrose has fixed composition (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁). A salad has visibly separate parts. Neon consists of a single element.
problems.a: (a) homogeneous mixture, (b) compound, (c) heterogeneous mixture, (d) element.

problems.q: A 5.00 g piece of an unknown metal displaces 1.85 mL of water. Find its density and say which metal it might be: aluminum (2.70 g/cm³), iron (7.87 g/cm³) or zinc (7.14 g/cm³).
problems.solution: ρ = 5.00 g / 1.85 mL = 2.70 g/mL, and 1 mL = 1 cm³.

problems.q: Report each result with the correct significant figures: (a) 0.0560 × 12.5 / 3.0, (b) 105.2 − 3.75 + 0.481.
problems.solution: (a) 0.0560 × 12.5 = 0.700; 0.700 / 3.0 = 0.233, limited by 3.0 to two significant figures: 0.23. (b) 105.2 − 3.75 + 0.481 = 101.931, limited by 105.2 to one decimal place: 101.9.

problems.q: A gold bar of dimensions 10.0 cm × 5.0 cm × 2.5 cm has density 19.3 g/cm³. What is its mass in kilograms, and its approximate value if gold costs $75 per gram?
problems.solution: V = 10.0 × 5.0 × 2.5 = 125 cm³. m = 19.3 × 125 = 2.4 × 10³ g = 2.4 kg (two significant figures, from 5.0 and 2.5). Value ≈ 2.4 × 10³ g × $75/g = $1.8 × 10⁵.

problems.q: The boiling point of helium is 4.2 K. Express it in °C and °F.
